claim: SNACS is a genetically encoded reporter for SnRK2 kinase activity that shows an increase in the ratio of yellow to cyan fluorescence emission by OST1/SnRK2.6-mediated phosphorylation of a defined serine residue.
source: This sensor, named SNACS, shows an increase in the ratio of yellow to cyan fluorescence emission by OST1/SnRK2.6-mediated phosphorylation of a defined serine residue in SNACS.
evidence: The abstract directly states the sensor's mechanism and function, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: ABA rapidly increases FRET efficiency in N. benthamiana leaf cells.
source: ABA rapidly increases FRET efficiency in N. benthamiana leaf cells and Arabidopsis guard cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 demonstrating time-resolved FRET ratio changes in response to ABA.

claim: ABA rapidly increases FRET efficiency in Arabidopsis guard cells.
source: ABA rapidly increases FRET efficiency in N. benthamiana leaf cells and Arabidopsis guard cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4 demonstrating ABA-induced FRET ratio increases in guard cells.

claim: Protein kinase inhibition decreases FRET efficiency in guard cells, providing direct experimental evidence that basal SnRK2 activity prevails in guard cells.
source: Interestingly, protein kinase inhibition decreases FRET efficiency in guard cells, providing direct experimental evidence that basal SnRK2 activity prevails in guard cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 6 showing K252a-induced reduction in SNACS FRET ratio.

claim: Elevated CO2 did not increase SNACS FRET ratios in guard cells.
source: Moreover, in contrast to ABA, the stomatal closing stimuli, elevated CO2 and MeJA, did not increase SNACS FRET ratios.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 8 showing no FRET ratio increases after high CO2 treatment.

claim: MeJA did not increase SNACS FRET ratios in guard cells.
source: Moreover, in contrast to ABA, the stomatal closing stimuli, elevated CO2 and MeJA, did not increase SNACS FRET ratios.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 7 showing no FRET ratio increases after MeJA treatment.

claim: Stomatal CO2 signaling requires basal ABA and SnRK2 signaling, but not SnRK2 activation.
source: These findings and gas exchange analyses of quintuple/sextuple ABA receptor mutants show that stomatal CO2 signaling requires basal ABA and SnRK2 signaling, but not SnRK2 activation.
evidence: Supported by SNACS imaging data showing no CO2-induced SnRK2 activation and gas exchange data from ABA receptor mutants.

claim: A recent model that CO2 signaling is mediated by PYL4/PYL5 ABA-receptors could not be supported in two independent labs.
source: A recent model that CO2 signaling is mediated by PYL4/PYL5 ABA-receptors could not be supported here in two independent labs.
evidence: Supported by gas exchange experiments in Figure 9 showing CO2 responses in quintuple and sextuple ABA receptor mutants lacking PYL4 and PYL5.

claim: Protein phosphorylation of downstream substrates by protein kinases is a central and critical molecular switch for activation of many cell biological processes.
source: Protein phosphorylation of downstream substrates by protein kinases is a central and critical molecular switch for activation of many cell biological processes (Ardito et al., 2017; Stone and Walker, 1995).
evidence: This is a general statement supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Investigation of protein kinase activities remains a challenge, particularly real-time measurements in living cells.
source: However, investigation of protein kinase activities remains a challenge, particularly real-time measurements in living cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field based on established knowledge.

claim: In-gel kinase assays are the most common method for measuring protein kinase activities using the (auto-)phosphorylation state of a kinase or a substrate as indicator of the kinase activity.
source: In-gel kinase assays are the most common method for measuring protein kinase activities using the (auto-)phosphorylation state of a kinase or a substrate as indicator of the kinase activity (Manning et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a statement about established methodology supported by citation.

claim: With in-gel kinase assays, it is difficult to track dynamic kinase activity in specific cell types or tissues, and time course measurements in living cells and subcellular analyses are not feasible.
source: With this method, it is difficult to track dynamic kinase activity in specific cell types or tissues, and time course measurements in living cells and subcellular analyses are not feasible (Aoki et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of in-gel kinase assays supported by citation.

claim: A first Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) biosensor reporting the activity of cAMP-dependent protein kinase A (PKA) was developed by R.Y. Tsien and colleagues.
source: To overcome this drawback, a first Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) biosensor reporting the activity of cAMP-dependent protein kinase A (PKA) was developed by R.Y. Tsien and colleagues (Zhang et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a historical statement about prior work supported by citation.

claim: The design of a FRET-based protein kinase biosensor includes a phosphorylatable substrate protein domain and a phosphorylation recognition domain that together can drive a conformational change between two fluorophores.
source: The design of a FRET-based protein kinase biosensor includes a phosphorylatable substrate protein domain and a phosphorylation recognition domain that together can drive a conformational change between two fluorophores (Sample et al., 2014; Ting et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2005; Gao and Zhang, 2008; Miyawaki and Tsien, 2000).
evidence: This describes the general design principle of FRET biosensors supported by multiple citations.

claim: In plants, only one protein kinase FRET biosensor has been reported to date, that senses plant MAP kinase activity using a MAPK substrate domain.
source: In plants, only one protein kinase FRET biosensor has been reported to date, that senses plant MAP kinase activity using a MAPK substrate domain (MAP kinase phosphatase, MKP1) and a FHA domain (Zaman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field in plant biology supported by citation.

claim: Abscisic acid (ABA) is a plant hormone which plays a central role in plant drought, cold and salinity stress tolerance.
source: Abscisic acid (ABA) is a plant hormone, which plays a central role in plant drought, cold and salinity stress tolerance (Cutler et al., 2010; Raghavendra et al., 2010; Zhu, 2016).
evidence: This is an established fact about ABA function supported by citations.

claim: SnRK2 protein kinases are members of a plant-specific serine/threonine kinase family that play critical roles in ABA signal transduction.
source: SnRK2 protein kinases (sucrose non-fermenting-1-related protein kinase 2s) are members of a plant-specific serine/threonine kinase family that play critical roles in ABA signal transduction (Fujii et al., 2007; Mustilli et al., 2002; Yoshida et al., 2002; Fujii and Zhu, 2009).
evidence: This is an established fact about SnRK2 kinases supported by citations.

claim: ABA activation of SnRK2 protein kinases has been found in several species including Vicia faba, rice, Arabidopsis, Glycine soja and Triticum polonicum.
source: ABA activation of SnRK2 protein kinases has been found in several species including Vicia faba (Li et al., 2000), rice (Kobayashi et al., 2004), Arabidopsis (Hrabak et al., 2003; Fujii and Zhu, 2009), Glycine soja (Yang et al., 2012) and Triticum polonicum (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about prior findings in multiple species supported by citations.

claim: In Arabidopsis, there are 10 SnRK2 family members (SnRK2.1–2.10) in the genome.
source: In Arabidopsis, there are 10 SnRK2 family members (SnRK2.1–2.10) in the genome.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the Arabidopsis genome based on established knowledge.

claim: Three SnRK2 protein kinases, SnRK2.2, SnRK2.3 and SnRK2.6/OST1, are strongly activated by ABA.
source: Three of these protein kinases, SnRK2.2, SnRK2.3 and SnRK2.6/OST1, are strongly activated by ABA.
evidence: This is an established fact about specific SnRK2 kinases based on prior research.

claim: The SnRK2.6/OST1 gene is expressed in stomatal guard cells.
source: The SnRK2.6/OST1 gene is expressed in stomatal guard cells (Mustilli et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a statement about gene expression supported by citation.

claim: SnRK2.6/OST1 mediates reduction of stomatal apertures and plays a pivotal role in ABA-induced stomatal closure.
source: SnRK2.6/OST1 mediates reduction of stomatal apertures and plays a pivotal role in ABA-induced stomatal closure (Yoshida et al., 2002; Mustilli et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an established fact about OST1 function supported by citations.

claim: SnRK2.6/OST1 is genetically required for rapid stomatal closure in response to elevation in the CO2 concentration.
source: In addition, SnRK2.6/OST1 is genetically required for rapid stomatal closure in response to elevation in the CO2 concentration (Xue et al., 2011; Merilo et al., 2013; Hsu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about genetic requirements supported by citations.

claim: SnRK2.6/OST1 is required for methyl jasmonate (MeJA)-induced stomatal closure.
source: Furthermore, SnRK2.6/OST1 is also required for methyl jasmonate (MeJA)-induced stomatal closure (Yin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about genetic requirements supported by citation.

claim: Whether MeJA or CO2 activate OST1/SnRK2.6 protein kinases in guard cells and whether CO2 rapidly activates ABA signaling remains controversial.
source: However, whether MeJA or CO2 activate OST1/SnRK2.6 protein kinases in guard cells and whether CO2 rapidly activates ABA signaling remains controversial.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Methyl jasmonate (MeJA)-induced stomatal closure has been shown in several species.
source: Studies have shown Methyl jasmonate (MeJA)-induced stomatal closure in several species (Herde and Pena-Cortes, 1997; Gehring, 1997; Suhita et al., 2004; Akter et al., 2012; Förster et al., 2019)
evidence: This is a statement about prior findings supported by citations.

claim: MeJA-induced stomatal closing is impaired in snrk2.6/ost1 mutants.
source: and that MeJA-induced stomatal closing is impaired in snrk2.6/ost1 mutants (Yin et al., 2016; Munemasa et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about mutant phenotypes supported by citations.

claim: Recent in-gel kinase assays with isolated guard cell protoplasts detected no MeJA-induced enhancement of OST1 kinase activity.
source: Unexpectedly, however, recent in-gel kinase assays with isolated guard cell protoplasts detected no MeJA-induced enhancement of OST1 kinase activity (Munemasa et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about prior experimental findings supported by citation.

claim: Classical research demonstrated that ABA enhances CO2-induced stomatal closing and vice versa.
source: Classical research demonstrated that ABA enhances CO2-induced stomatal closing and vice versa (Raschke, 1975; Raschke et al., 1976).
evidence: This is a statement about classical findings supported by citations.

claim: Plants have previously been found to have higher basal ABA concentrations in guard cells than in leaf mesophyll cells.
source: In addition, plants have previously been found to have higher basal ABA concentrations in guard cells than in leaf mesophyll cells (Lahr and Raschke, 1988).
evidence: This is a statement about prior findings supported by citation.

claim: ost1 mutant alleles have been shown to impair CO2-induced stomatal closing in intact leaves and intact plants.
source: ost1 mutant alleles have been shown to impair CO2-induced stomatal closing in intact leaves and intact plants (Xue et al., 2011; Merilo et al., 2013), but not as strongly as ABA-induced stomatal closing (Hsu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about mutant phenotypes supported by citations.

claim: Recent in-gel kinase assays show no CO2 activation of SnRK2 kinases in purified guard cells protoplasts.
source: Unexpectedly, however, recent in-gel kinase assays show no CO2 activation of SnRK2 kinases in purified guard cells protoplasts (Hsu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about prior experimental findings supported by citation.

claim: Whether ABA-SnRK2 signal transduction is directly activated by CO2 elevation remains controversial.
source: Moreover, whether ABA-SnRK2 signal transduction is directly activated by CO2 elevation remains controversial (Chater et al., 2015; Merilo et al., 2013; Hsu et al., 2018; Dittrich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field supported by citations.

claim: In-gel kinase assay analyses have shown that ABA rapidly activates OST1/SnRK2.6/AAPK protein kinases using purified guard cell protoplasts.
source: In-gel kinase assay analyses have shown that ABA rapidly activates OST1/SnRK2.6/AAPK protein kinases using purified guard cell protoplasts (Li et al., 2000; Mustilli et al., 2002; Hsu et al., 2018; Li and Assmann, 1996; Mori and Muto, 1997).
evidence: This is a statement about prior experimental findings supported by citations.

claim: ABA-activated SnRK2 protein kinases phosphorylate several downstream substrates including the SLAC1 anion channel and transcription factors.
source: ABA-activated SnRK2 protein kinases phosphorylate several downstream substrates including the SLAC1 anion channel and transcription factors (Takahashi et al., 2013; Munemasa et al., 2019; Geiger et al., 2009; Furihata et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a statement about SnRK2 substrates supported by citations.

claim: ABA-responsive kinase substrate 1 (AKS1) is a basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) transcription factor.
source: ABA-responsive kinase substrate 1 (AKS1) is a basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) transcription factor (Takahashi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about AKS1 identity supported by citation.

claim: AKS1 was demonstrated to be phosphorylated by SnRK2s in response to ABA in Arabidopsis guard cells, as an endogenous phosphorylation substrate.
source: AKS1 was demonstrated to be phosphorylated by SnRK2s in response to ABA in Arabidopsis guard cells, as an endogenous phosphorylation substrate (Takahashi et al., 2017; Takahashi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about AKS1 phosphorylation supported by citations.

claim: ABA rapidly induces 14-3-3 protein binding to AKS1 in a phosphorylation-dependent manner in guard cells.
source: Moreover, ABA rapidly induces 14-3-3 protein binding to AKS1 in a phosphorylation-dependent manner in guard cells (Takahashi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about ABA-induced protein interactions supported by citation.

claim: 14-3-3 proteins are conserved proteins in eukaryotes and known for binding to target proteins upon phosphorylation.
source: 14-3-3 proteins are conserved proteins in eukaryotes and known for binding to target proteins upon phosphorylation.
evidence: This is an established fact about 14-3-3 proteins based on general knowledge.

claim: 14-3-3 proteins recognize two typical 14-3-3 binding motifs, which in AKS1 are the Ser-30 residue and Ser-157 residue.
source: 14-3-3 proteins recognize two typical 14-3-3 binding motifs, which in AKS1 are the Ser-30 residue and Ser-157 residue (Takahashi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about 14-3-3 binding motifs supported by citation.

claim: The AKS1 (S30A/S157A) mutant protein does not bind to the 14-3-3 protein GF14phi.
source: The AKS1 (S30A/S157A) mutant protein does not bind to the 14-3-3 protein GF14phi (Takahashi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about mutant protein interactions supported by citation.

claim: The OST1/SnRK2.6 protein kinase can phosphorylate the SNACS sensor, but not the SNACS-S785A mutant isoform.
source: The results showed that the OST1/SnRK2.6 protein kinase can phosphorylate this sensor, but not the SNACS-S785A mutant isoform (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by in vitro phosphorylation assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The unrelated Ca2+-dependent protein kinase, CPK6, did not measurably phosphorylate the wild-type SNACS or S785A mutant.
source: Furthermore, the unrelated Ca2+-dependent protein kinase, CPK6, did not measurably phosphorylate the wild-type SNACS or S785A mutant (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by in vitro phosphorylation assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: SNACS showed an increase in YPet emission by an average of 11.8% and a decrease of Turquoise GL emission by 12.96% in the presence of OST1/SnRK2.6 compared to SNACS alone upon Turquoise GL excitation.
source: The SNACS showed an increase in YPet emission (average data points, 525–531 nm) by an average of 11.8% and a decrease of Turquoise GL emission (average data points, 471–477 nm) by 12.96% in the presence of OST1/SnRK2.6 compared to the SNACS alone upon Turquoise GL excitation (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by in vitro FRET assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In the presence of the inactive mutant isoform OST1/SnRK2.6 (OST1D140A) protein kinase, no clear FRET ratio increase was found.
source: In addition, in the presence of the inactive mutant isoform OST1/SnRK2.6 (OST1D140A) protein kinase as a control, no clear FRET ratio increase was found (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by in vitro FRET assay data shown in Figure 1E and supplementary figures.

claim: The mutant SNACSS785A isoform with the AKS1 Ser-30-Ala mutation did not show FRET ratio changes after an incubation with the OST1/SnRK2.6 protein kinase upon Turquoise GL excitation.
source: Consistent with the above results, the mutant SNACSS785A isoform with the AKS1 Ser-30-Ala mutation did not show FRET ratio changes after an incubation with the OST1/SnRK2.6 protein kinase upon Turquoise GL excitation (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by in vitro FRET assay data shown in Figure 1F and supplementary figures.

claim: SnRK2.3 induced a SNACS FRET ratio increase.
source: In additional experiments, SnRK2.3, another protein of SnRK2 family, induced a SNACS FRET ratio increase as well (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by in vitro FRET assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The highly active CPK6 protein kinase did not increase the FRET ratio of SNACS.
source: In contrast, the highly active CPK6 protein kinase (Brandt et al., 2012), did not increase the FRET ratio (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by in vitro FRET assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The application of ABA caused time-resolved emission ratio increases in N. benthamiana epidermal cells.
source: Interestingly, the application of ABA caused time-resolved emission ratio (YPet to Turquoise GL emission) increases in N. benthamiana epidermal cells (Figure 2A,C,D) (n = 3 experiments; 11–13 cells imaged in each experiment).
evidence: Supported by time-resolved FRET imaging data shown in Figure 2.

claim: EtOH treatments did not induce measurable emission ratio increases of SNACS in N. benthamiana epidermal cells.
source: EtOH treatments did not induce measurable emission ratio increases of SNACS (Figure 2B, n = 3 experiments; 4–7 cells imaged in each experiment).
evidence: Supported by control experiment data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Application of 20 µM ABA induced a clear time-dependent increase in the FRET ratio in Arabidopsis guard cells expressing SNACS in the pUBQ10:OST1-HF/ost1-3 background.
source: Using a genetic background in which a tagged version of OST1 was expressed in the OST1 T-DNA insertion allele ost1-3 (pUBQ10:OST1-HF/ost1-3) (Yoshida et al., 2002; Waadt et al., 2015), application of 20 µM ABA induced a clear time-dependent increase in the FRET ratio, which reached stable saturation 2 to 4 min after application (Figure 3A,C to E, p=0.015, paired t-test, before ABA time point 3 min vs. after ABA time point 10 min; All following imaging analyses were evaluated by paired t-tests).
evidence: Supported by time-resolved FRET imaging data in guard cells shown in Figure 3.

claim: Ethanol control applications showed no clear YPet/Turquoise GL emission ratio change in Arabidopsis guard cells.
source: Ethanol control applications showed no clear YPet/Turquoise GL emission ratio change (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by control experiment data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: SNACS protein is either absent from the nucleus or is expressed at lower levels than in the cytoplasm.
source: Image analyses suggest that SNACS protein is either absent from the nucleus or is expressed at lower levels than in the cytoplasm, with fluorescence possibly 'bleeding through' from the cytoplasm to the nucleus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the Col-0 (wild-type) background, expression of SNACS showed ABA-induced emission ratio increases in guard cells.
source: Similar to the above experiments (Figure 3), in the Col-0 (wild-type) background, expression of SNACS showed ABA-induced emission ratio increases in guard cells (Figure 4A and D, n = 24 stomata, p=2 × 10−12 3 min vs. 10 min time points).
evidence: Supported by FRET imaging data in guard cells shown in Figure 4A and D.

claim: In transgenic lines expressing the mutant SNACSS785A, no clear increases in the ratio of YPet to Turquoise GL emission ratio were observed after ABA application.
source: In transgenic lines expressing the mutant SNACSS785A, that corresponds to the Ser-30-Ala mutation in AKS1, no clear increases in the ratio of YPet to Turquoise GL emission ratio were observed after ABA application (Figure 4C and G; n = 9 stomata (4C), p=0.892, 3 min vs. 10 min; n = 12 stomata (4G), p=0.184, 3 min vs. 10 min).
evidence: Supported by FRET imaging data with mutant sensor shown in Figure 4C and G.

claim: The phosphorylation site Ser 785 residue of SNACS is necessary for ABA-induced increases in the ratio of YPet to Turquoise GL emission in plant cells.
source: These data indicate that the phosphorylation site Ser 785 residue of SNACS (Figure 4C and G) is necessary for ABA-induced increases in the ratio of YPet to Turquoise GL emission in plant cells.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of wild-type SNACS and SNACSS785A mutant responses to ABA.

claim: ABA caused clear fluorescence emission ratio increases in ost1/snrk2.6 guard cells.
source: Interestingly, ABA caused clear fluorescence emission ratio increases in ost1/snrk2.6 guard cells (Figure 5B; n = 14 stomata, p=3.2 × 10−7 3 min vs. 10 min).
evidence: Supported by FRET imaging data in ost1 mutant guard cells shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In the ost1/snrk2.6 background, ABA induced slower emission ratio increases compared to Col-0 guard cells.
source: Compared to the Col-0 guard cells, in the ost1/snrk2.6 background ABA induced slower emission ratio increases (Figure 5A and B; n = 12 stomata (5A), p=2.4 × 10−6 3 min vs. 10 min).
evidence: Supported by comparison of FRET imaging data between Col-0 and ost1 mutant shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: In snrk2.2/2.3 double mutant guard cells, ABA induced FRET ratio increases.
source: In snrk2.2/2.3 double mutant guard cells, ABA induced FRET ratio increases were observed (Figure 5C, n = 20 stomata (5C), p=5.7 × 10−9 3 min vs. 10 min).
evidence: Supported by FRET imaging data in snrk2.2/2.3 mutant guard cells shown in Figure 5C.

claim: No ABA-induced ratio increase was observed in the snrk2.2/2.3/2.6 triple mutant guard cells.
source: Notably, no ABA-induced ratio increase was observed in the snrk2.2/2.3/2.6 triple mutant guard cells, which suggests that SnRK2 activity is required for ABA-induced SNACS-dependent FRET ratio changes in planta (Figure 5D, n = 9 stomata, p=0.122 3 min vs. 10 min).
evidence: Supported by FRET imaging data in triple mutant guard cells shown in Figure 5D.

claim: SnRK2 activity is required for ABA-induced SNACS-dependent FRET ratio changes in planta.
source: Notably, no ABA-induced ratio increase was observed in the snrk2.2/2.3/2.6 triple mutant guard cells, which suggests that SnRK2 activity is required for ABA-induced SNACS-dependent FRET ratio changes in planta (Figure 5D, n = 9 stomata, p=0.122 3 min vs. 10 min).
evidence: Inferred from the lack of ABA response in the triple mutant.

claim: 10 µM K252a application resulted in a time-resolved drop in the FRET emission ratio in Arabidopsis guard cells.
source: We found that 10 µM K252a application resulted in a time-resolved drop in the FRET emission ratio in Arabidopsis guard cells (Figure 6A; n = 13 stomata (6A), p=4.9 × 10−6 3 min vs.10 min; n = 11 stomata (6B, controls), p=0.158 3 min vs. 10 min).
evidence: Supported by FRET imaging data with K252a treatment shown in Figure 6A.

claim: ABA did not induce measurable emission ratio increases after K252a application.
source: In addition, ABA did not induce measurable emission ratio increases after K252a application, suggesting that ABA-induced emission ratio increases are caused by K252a-sensitive protein kinase activity in vivo (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by FRET imaging data showing no ABA response after K252a treatment in Figure 6A.

claim: After ABA treatment and subsequent K252a exposure, the FRET emission ratio decreased, suggesting that SNACS can reversibly report protein kinase activity.
source: Interestingly, after ABA treatment and subsequent K252a exposure, the FRET emission ratio decreased, suggesting that SNACS can reversibly report protein kinase activity (Figure 6C; n = 10 stomata (6C), p=0.0004 3 min vs.10 min, p=0.0001 10 min vs. 20 min; n = 8 stomata (6D, controls), p=0.00003 3 min vs.10 min, p=0.836 10 min vs. 20 min).
evidence: Supported by FRET imaging data showing reversibility in Figure 6C.

claim: W7 does not have a clear effect on ABA-induced OST1/SnRK2.6 activation in Arabidopsis mesophyll cell protoplasts.
source: In-gel kinase assays showed that W7 does not have a clear effect on ABA-induced OST1/SnRK2.6 activation in Arabidopsis mesophyll cell protoplasts (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in-gel kinase assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: K252a inhibited ABA-induced in-gel kinase activity.
source: In controls K252a inhibited ABA-induced in-gel kinase activity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in-gel kinase assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: W7 treatment did not cause FRET ratio changes in guard cells.
source: We found no FRET ratio changes upon W7 treatment (Figure 6E and F; n = 8 stomata (6E), p=0.988 3 min vs.10 min; n = 7 stomata (6F, controls), p=0.348 3 min vs.10 min).
evidence: Supported by FRET imaging data with W7 treatment shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: After W7 exposure, application of ABA caused ABA-induced FRET shifts.
source: After W7 exposure, application of ABA caused ABA-induced FRET shifts (Figure 6E and F; p=1.1 × 10−9 (6E), p=7.4 × 10−6 (6F), 10 min vs. 20 min).
evidence: Supported by FRET imaging data showing ABA response after W7 treatment in Figure 6E and F.

claim: SNACS is a reversible protein kinase activity reporter.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that SNACS is a reversible protein kinase activity reporter and that SNACS can report basal SnRK2 activity in vivo, that is down-regulated upon kinase inhibition.
evidence: Inferred from K252a experiments showing both decrease in FRET ratio and reversibility.

claim: SNACS can report basal SnRK2 activity in vivo, that is down-regulated upon kinase inhibition.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that SNACS is a reversible protein kinase activity reporter and that SNACS can report basal SnRK2 activity in vivo, that is down-regulated upon kinase inhibition.
evidence: Inferred from K252a-induced decrease in FRET ratio in the absence of exogenous ABA.

claim: Methyl jasmonate (MeJA) has been previously reported to induce stomatal closure.
source: Methyl jasmonate (MeJA) has been previously reported to induce stomatal closure (Herde and Pena-Cortes, 1997; Gehring, 1997; Suhita et al., 2004; Akter et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about prior findings supported by citations.

claim: The OST1/SnRK2.6 kinase is required for MeJA-induced stomatal closure.
source: The OST1/SnRK2.6 kinase is required for MeJA-induced stomatal closure (Yin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about genetic requirements supported by citation.

claim: Exogenous application of MeJA did not result in robust FRET emission ratio changes in Arabidopsis guard cells.
source: Exogenous application of MeJA did not result in robust FRET emission ratio changes in Arabidopsis guard cells (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1; n = 9 stomata (7A), p=0.981 3 min vs. 15 min, p=0.896 3 min vs. 25 min; n = 12 stomata (7B, controls), p=0.553 3 min vs. 15 min, p=0.664, 3 min vs. 25 min).
evidence: Supported by FRET imaging data with MeJA treatment shown in Figure 7.

claim: In the presence of MeJA, subsequent application of ABA caused increases in the SNACS emission ratio.
source: Furthermore, in the presence of MeJA, subsequent application of ABA caused increases in the SNACS emission ratio in these experiments (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by FRET imaging data showing ABA response after MeJA treatment in Figure 7.

claim: snrk2.6/ost1 mutant alleles show impaired and slowed CO2-induced stomatal closure.
source: snrk2.6/ost1 mutant alleles show impaired and slowed CO2-induced stomatal closure (Xue et al., 2011; Merilo et al., 2013; Hsu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about mutant phenotypes supported by citations.

claim: A recent study suggests that CO2 elevation does not activate SnRK2.6/OST1 protein kinases using in-gel kinase assays with isolated Arabidopsis guard cell protoplasts.
source: Interestingly, a recent study suggests that CO2 elevation does not activate SnRK2.6/OST1 protein kinases using in-gel kinase assays with isolated Arabidopsis guard cell protoplasts (Hsu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about prior findings supported by citation.

claim: FRET emission ratios showed no measurable increases after a 40 min incubation with high CO2 buffer in guard cells.
source: FRET emission ratios showed no measurable increases after a 40 min incubation with the high CO2 buffer (Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A, n = 9 stomata, p=0.184 3 min vs. 15 min).
evidence: Supported by FRET imaging data with high CO2 treatment shown in Figure 8A.

claim: After high CO2 treatment, 20 µM ABA caused rapid FRET ratio increases in guard cells.
source: After high CO2 treatment, 20 µM ABA was added to the buffer. We observed rapid FRET ratio increases in response to ABA (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by FRET imaging data showing ABA response after CO2 treatment in Figure 8A.

claim: No clear FRET ratio increases were detected for continuous 30 min low CO2 exposure (115 ppm).
source: No clear FRET ratio increases were detected for continuous 30 min low CO2 exposure (115 ppm). Subsequent exposure to 20 µM ABA caused ratio increases (Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B, n = 14 stomata, p=5.9 × 10−6 20 min vs. 35 min).
evidence: Supported by FRET imaging data with low CO2 treatment shown in Figure 8B.

claim: CO2-induced stomatal closing is >80% completed within 15 to 20 min of a CO2 concentration elevation in wild-type (Col-0) Arabidopsis.
source: CO2-induced stomatal closing is >80% completed within 15 to 20 min of a CO2 concentration elevation in wild-type (Col-0) Arabidopsis (Young et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about stomatal kinetics supported by citation.

claim: No dramatic ABAleon2.15 emission ratio change was observed upon increasing the CO2 concentration from 115 ppm to 1170 ppm.

claim: Exposure to 20 µM ABA caused a rapid reduction in the ABAleon2.15 FRET ratio, which corresponds to an increase in cellular ABA concentration.
source: At the end of these experiments, intact abaxial leaf epidermises were exposed to 20 µM ABA, which caused a rapid reduction in the ABAleon2.15 FRET ratio (Figure 8C,D and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C), which corresponds to an increase in cellular ABA concentration (Waadt et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by ABAleon2.15 imaging data showing ABA response in Figure 8C and D, with interpretation based on citation.

claim: No clear rapid increase in the cellular ABA concentration of guard cells was found within the time frame in which CO2-induced stomatal closing occurs.

claim: A recent study has suggested that CO2-induced stomatal closing requires PYL4 and PYL5 ABA receptors.

claim: All tested plant lines displayed stomatal closure in response to changing the CO2 concentration from ambient (400 ppm) to 800 ppm.

claim: ABA receptor sextuple mutant plants displayed 5.2 times higher pre-CO2-treatment stomatal conductance compared to wild-type.
source: ABA receptor sextuple mutant plants displayed 5.2 times higher pre-CO2-treatment stomatal conductance compared to wild-type (Figure 9A and C).

claim: ABA receptor quintuple pyl-11458 and pyl-12458 mutants maintained 2.3 and 2.9 times higher pretreatment stomatal conductances compared to wild-type.
source: ABA receptor quintuple pyl-11458 and pyl-12458 mutants maintained 2.3 and 2.9 times higher pretreatment stomatal conductances compared to wild-type (Figure 9A and C).
evidence: Supported by gas exchange data shown in Figure 9A and C.

claim: After application of elevated CO2, the stomatal conductance of all ABA receptor mutant lines decreased to a similar or even higher extent than in wild-type plants.
source: After application of elevated CO2, the stomatal conductance of all ABA receptor mutant lines decreased to a similar or even higher extent than in wild-type plants even though their stomatal conductances remained higher after 50 min in elevated CO2 (Figure 9A and C).
evidence: Supported by gas exchange data shown in Figure 9A and C.

claim: Stomatal responses to CO2 shifts from 400 to 800 ppm were clearly delayed in PYR/RCAR sextuple mutant plants as indicated by a roughly twice longer half-response time.
source: Stomatal responses to CO2 shifts from 400 to 800 ppm were clearly delayed in PYR/RCAR sextuple mutant plants as indicated by a roughly twice longer half-response time (Figure 9D), consistent with previous findings (Hsu et al., 2018).

claim: In absolute units, PYR/RCAR quintuple mutant pyl-12458 and sextuple mutant pyl-112458 plants displayed a larger absolute reduction in stomatal conductance in response to high CO2 than wild-type plants.

evidence: Supported by analysis of gas exchange data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: pyl-11458 quintuple mutant leaves showed stomatal opening in response to 125 µmol m−2 s−1 light.
source: In these experiments, pyl-11458 quintuple mutant leaves showed stomatal opening in response to 125 µmol m−2 s−1 light as expected.

claim: After light-induced stomatal opening, CO2 elevation showed similar CO2-induced stomatal closing in the wild-type (Col-0) background as in the pyl-11458 quintuple mutant that lacks PYL4 and PYL5.

claim: In complementation lines expressing PYL4, PYL5 or PYL1 under control of the guard cell pGC1 promoter, no clear enhancement of the final CO2 response was observed.

evidence: Supported by gas exchange data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2B to D.

source: Thus in the two laboratories in which CO2-regulation of stomatal conductance was investigated in intact plants in the present study (EM and HK lab and JS lab), we could not confirm that the absence of PYL4 and PYL5 disrupts the stomatal CO2 response (Dittrich et al., 2019).

evidence: This is a statement about the practical requirements of in-gel kinase assays based on established methodology.

source: FRET imaging with SNACS permits single cell-type imaging in real-time, compared to the need to purify very large numbers of cells and isolate extracts for each in-gel kinase assay lane.
evidence: This is a comparison of methodological advantages based on the experimental approach.

source: HAB1 (also named AtP2C-HA) (Chérel et al., 2002; Saez et al., 2004; Leonhardt et al., 2004), a type 2C protein phosphatase involved in ABA signal transduction, does not appear to dephosphorylate the Ser-30 residue of the AKS1 transcription factor (Takahashi et al., 2017).

claim: PP2A phosphatases may dephosphorylate AKS1.

evidence: This is a statement about prior findings supported by citation.

claim: These findings may support a recently proposed calcium-dependent parallel MeJA response pathway.
source: These findings may support a recently proposed calcium-dependent parallel MeJA response pathway (Förster et al., 2019).

claim: Basal SnRK2 activity, functioning parallel to the CO2 signal transduction branch, is required for and/or could amplify CO2 signaling.
